<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

  /* Reading mode hides the chrome and the empty .arxiv-html-header marker: the pinned JS reads
     the marker's display to know which way to toggle. The marker draws no box. */
  .arxiv-html-header { display: contents; }
  html[data-reading-mode="enabled"] :is(.arxiv-html-site-chrome, .arxiv-html-header, .ds-site-footer) { display: none; }
  /* The paper controls' icons are blocks, so they sit centred (the pinned JS shows the theme
     icon by making its span a block). */
  .arxiv-html-site-chrome .ds-site-header-tools svg { display: block; width: 18px; height: 18px; flex-shrink: 0; fill: currentColor; }
  /* ar5iv dims every image in dark mode and puts it on a white wash, for paper figures;
     arXiv's own render as they are (the logo on the bar, the funder logos on their white
     chips). Important: ar5iv's dark rules are unlayered, as specific as
     :root:not([data-theme]) img:not(.ltx_no_dark_filter). */
  :is(.ds-site-header, .ds-site-footer) img { filter: none !important; }
  .ds-site-header img { background-color: transparent !important; }

  /* Wide (the theme's 1280px): the theme lays the body out as a grid whose full-width top rows
     were the band's and its sticky reader bar's. The band takes the first and scrolls away; the
     header, the paper's bar (no site navigation, the paper's controls), takes the second and
     stays in view, the one sticky bar, with the anchor clearance that requires (DESIGN-POLICIES).
     The controls show their names. */
  @media (min-width: 1280px) {
    html { scroll-padding-top: 80px; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome { display: contents; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome > #ds-announcement { grid-area: announce; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome > .ds-site-header { grid-area: header; position: sticky; top: 0; z-index: 3; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome .tool-icon { display: none; }
  }
  /* Narrow: the header scrolls away, and the controls show icons (names kept for screen
     readers; Why HTML? goes). The theme's contents panel is fixed below where its old sticky
     bar was, and hidden only once the reader has closed it, so until then it is an invisible box
     over the header and the paper: it shows only while open, under the chrome, in its place in
     the page. The paper's footer (build logs, reporting instructions) keeps the text's side
     inset; the theme gives it none, so it met the screen edges. */
  @media (max-width: 1279px) {
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome .tool-wide { display: none; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome .tool-label { position: absolute; width: 1px; height: 1px; overflow: hidden; clip: rect(0 0 0 0); white-space: nowrap; }
    html:not([data-toc-display="block"]) .ltx_page_navbar { display: none; }
    .ltx_page_navbar { position: absolute; top: auto; }
    .arxiv-html-footer { padding-inline: 1rem; }
  }

<article class="ltx_document">
<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document">MacArena: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents 
<br class="ltx_break">on an Online macOS Environment</h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">
<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Victor Muryn
</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>MacPaw Research, Kyiv, Ukraine
</span>

</span></span></span></span>

<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>MacPaw Research, Kyiv, Ukraine
</span>
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_email"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Correspondence to: </span><a href="mailto:mshamrai@macpaw.com">mshamrai@macpaw.com</a>
</span></span></span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">

</span></span></span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Yehor Khodysko
</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>MacPaw Research, Kyiv, Ukraine
</span></span></span></span></div>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Computer-use agents (CUAs) operate graphical user interfaces (GUIs) through vision and control primitives, and their capabilities have advanced rapidly, driven in part by standardized online evaluation benchmarks such as OSWorld, which serve both as evaluation tools and as training environments for reinforcement learning. However, macOS remains underserved in this landscape: the only existing benchmark, macOSWorld, covers a narrow slice of first-party applications with simpler tasks, and runs on x86 virtual machines incompatible with Apple Silicon. We introduce MacArena, a benchmark of 421 manually verified tasks spanning 50 applications that combines a curated port of OSWorld tasks, content sourced from macOSWorld, and 49 new macOS-native tasks, all running on Apple’s native Virtualization framework on Apple Silicon. We argue that macOS presents distinct GUI challenges beyond what Linux-based benchmarks capture, and our evaluation supports this claim: strong model performance on existing benchmarks can reflect familiarity with task distributions rather than genuine cross-platform GUI competence. Notably, model rankings invert between ported and macOS-native tasks, with a leading model trailing by over 26% on the MacArena subset, suggesting that macOS poses a genuinely harder environment for current GUI agents<span id="footnote1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup>
          <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">1</span>
          
          
          
          
          
          
          
        Code available online <a href="https://github.com/MacPaw/MacArena" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://github.com/MacPaw/MacArena</a></span></span></span>.</p>
  
</div>
<div class="ltx_keywords">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_keywords">Keywords: </h6>benchmark, computer-use agents, macOS, verifiable reward, ICML
</div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<figure id="S1.F1" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2606.06560v1/macarena_hero.svg" id="S1.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/215;" width="476" height="215"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S1.F1.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 1</span>: </span><span id="S1.F1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Overview of MacArena. Tasks are drawn from three sources: OSWorld (ported to macOS), macOSWorld, and 49 newly collected macOS-native tasks, totaling 421 human-verified tasks across 50 applications. At each timestep, the agent receives a screenshot and an accessibility tree as observations and produces an action executed within an Apple Silicon VM running via Apple’s Virtualization framework. An execution-based evaluator inspects the final environment state to assign a score <math id="S1.F1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r\in[0,1]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r\in[0,1]</annotation></semantics></math></span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Computer-use agents (CUAs) are systems capable of interacting with graphical user interfaces (GUIs) through direct manipulation — clicking, dragging, and typing on visible on-screen elements <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sager et al., 2026</a>; <a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Nguyen et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. CUAs operate directly on the pixel-level representations that human users see, enabling them to navigate applications, complete multi-step tasks, and respond to dynamic interface states <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zheng et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. Their ability to generalize across diverse software environments without requiring programmatic access to underlying systems positions them as a promising direction toward general-purpose digital assistants capable of executing real-world computer tasks on behalf of users.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Benchmarking CUA capabilities has been an active research area, with several interactive evaluation environments proposed in recent years. OSWorld <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xie et al., 2024</a>)</cite> established the leading cross-platform benchmark, spanning Linux and Windows, using real applications and executable tasks. Yet, macOS remains underserved as an evaluation target. The only existing macOS benchmark, macOSWorld <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, covers a narrow slice of the platform’s task space: UI navigation sequences are simpler, and task specifications are less ambiguous than those found in cross-platform benchmarks. Coverage is also limited almost exclusively to built-in applications, leaving a wide range of commonly used third-party software unevaluated — a significant gap given how central such software is to real-world macOS usage. Furthermore, macOSWorld relies on x86-based virtual machines, making it incompatible with the entire modern Apple Silicon lineup and unable to reflect the performance characteristics of current hardware. This raises a broader question: whether macOS presents distinct challenges for GUI agents that go beyond what existing Linux-based benchmarks capture.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">To address these gaps, we introduce <span id="S1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">MacArena</span>, a benchmark for evaluating computer-use agents on macOS (Figure <a href="#S1.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ MacArena: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on an Online macOS Environment" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>). MacArena is built from three sources: a curated port of tasks from OSWorld to macOS, a set of tasks sourced from macOSWorld, and 49 novel macOS-specific tasks that increase task complexity and broaden coverage to non-standard applications.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Our main contributions are:</p>
<ul id="S1.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">A large-scale macOS CUA benchmark</span> of 421 high-quality tasks, combining manually ported OSWorld tasks with verified macOSWorld tasks and 49 new macOS-specific tasks into a unified evaluation suite.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Human verification of all tasks</span>, ensuring each task is executable, unambiguous, and correctly specified, providing a higher-quality signal than automated task generation or partial review.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Full reproducibility</span>, with all code publicly released to enable community extension of the benchmark.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Evaluation of models</span>, establishing baseline results and surfacing strengths and limitations of existing CUAs on macOS.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Our evaluation establishes baseline results for current CUAs on macOS and reveals a consistent pattern: performance degrades across all evaluated models relative to Linux, suggesting macOS poses a genuinely harder environment for current GUI agents.</p>
</div>
</section>

<section id="S2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.1 </span>GUI Agents and Computer-Use Systems</h3>

<div id="S2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Early GUI agents were built around prompt-based pipelines that combined frontier vision-language models with modular planning and memory components. Systems such as UFO <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2025</a>)</cite> and SeeAct <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zheng et al., 2024</a>)</cite> demonstrated that GPT-4V could complete desktop and web tasks by reasoning over screenshots, while multi-agent frameworks decomposed tasks into subtasks handled by specialized subagents. Though effective in constrained settings, these systems were limited by the capabilities of the underlying models and the overhead of multi-step orchestration.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">A second line of work focused on improving visual grounding, the ability to precisely localize UI elements from natural language descriptions. CogAgent <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hong et al., 2024</a>)</cite> introduced a dual-encoder architecture trained specifically on GUI layouts, and subsequent models developed dedicated grounding modules that allowed agents to click and interact with greater spatial precision. This grounding capability became a prerequisite for reliable performance on complex desktop tasks.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">More recently, end-to-end trained agents have largely superseded prompt-based pipelines. Models such as UI-TARS <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qin et al., 2025</a>)</cite> and Aguvis <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xu et al., 2024</a>)</cite> are trained natively on large collections of GUI interaction trajectories across desktop, web, and mobile platforms, achieving strong generalization without relying on external orchestration. These single-model agents are simpler to deploy and have become the dominant paradigm for GUI agent development.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Reinforcement learning has emerged as a further lever for improving agent performance. DigiRL <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bai et al., 2024</a>)</cite> demonstrated offline-to-online RL fine-tuning on Android tasks, and ComputerRL <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lai et al., 2025</a>)</cite> scaled online RL to desktop environments using thousands of parallel virtual machines. UI-TARS-2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2025</a>)</cite> extended this with a multi-turn RL framework that generates training trajectories at scale. Across all of this work, OSWorld and AndroidWorld have served as the primary training and evaluation environments, underscoring the absence of a comparable macOS benchmark for desktop GUI research.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.2 </span>Computer Use Benchmarks</h3>

<div id="S2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Before interactive benchmarks, researchers developed offline datasets to evaluate agents on static screenshots. Mind2Web <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Deng et al., 2023</a>)</cite> and AITW <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Rawles et al., 2023</a>)</cite> collected large sets of human demonstrations for web and mobile navigation, enabling supervised training of GUI policies. ScreenSpot <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cheng et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, ScreenSpot-V2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wu et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, and ScreenSpot-Pro <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2025</a>)</cite> established benchmarks focused specifically on element localization, the ability to map a natural language instruction to the correct location on a screen. GUIrilla <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Garkot et al., 2026</a>)</cite> extended this to macOS, providing localization annotations across a wide range of third-party applications. While these offline benchmarks remain useful for model development, they do not capture the sequential decision-making, error recovery, and dynamic environment feedback that define real-world agent behavior, and therefore do not measure whether an agent can complete tasks in a live environment.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">OSWorld <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xie et al., 2024</a>)</cite> is the most comprehensive existing interactive benchmark, covering Linux and Windows with real applications, multi-step tasks, and automated grading based on functional outcomes. Tasks are initialized from virtual machine snapshots. OSWorld has become the standard environment for both training and evaluating desktop GUI agents. For macOS specifically, macOSWorld <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2025</a>)</cite> introduced a benchmark targeting Apple’s built-in applications, such as Finder, Safari, and Calendar. Yet its tasks tend to be simpler, and more narrowly defined than those in OSWorld, with coverage limited almost entirely to first-party software.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Hardware compatibility compounds this limitation. Following Apple’s 2020 transition away from Intel processors, x86-based macOS environments are increasingly misaligned with real-world usage: Apple Silicon now powers the entire Mac lineup, and Intel-based machines are no longer manufactured. Yet macOSWorld was designed around x86 virtual machines with no native Apple Silicon support. While cloud-based evaluation on Apple Silicon hardware (e.g., via EC2 Mac instances) is technically possible, it introduces significant cost overhead that makes large-scale benchmarking and RL training pipelines impractical.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">MacArena addresses these gaps directly. macOS presents distinct challenges for GUI agents: from its application conventions and complex window management to the widespread use of third-party software, that existing benchmarks leave largely unexamined. As shown in Table <a href="#S2.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 2 Related Work ‣ MacArena: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on an Online macOS Environment" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, MacArena is the only macOS online benchmark combining third-party application coverage with full manual verification.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>MacArena Environment</h2>

<tr id="S3.T2.5.15" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S3.T2.5.15.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_bb ltx_border_t" style="padding-top:1pt;padding-bottom:1pt;" rowspan="3"><span id="S3.T2.5.15.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Terminal</span></td>
<td id="S3.T2.5.15.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_t" style="padding-top:1pt;padding-bottom:1pt;"><span id="S3.T2.5.15.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">WAIT</span></td>
<td id="S3.T2.5.15.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_t" style="padding-top:1pt;padding-bottom:1pt;">—</td>
<td id="S3.T2.5.15.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_t" style="padding-top:1pt;padding-bottom:1pt;">Sleep until next action</td></tr>
<tr id="S3.T2.5.16" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S3.T2.5.16.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left" style="padding-top:1pt;padding-bottom:1pt;"><span id="S3.T2.5.16.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">FAIL</span></td>
<td id="S3.T2.5.16.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left" style="padding-top:1pt;padding-bottom:1pt;">—</td>
<td id="S3.T2.5.16.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left" style="padding-top:1pt;padding-bottom:1pt;">Signal task cannot be completed</td></tr>
<tr id="S3.T2.5.17" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S3.T2.5.17.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_bb" style="padding-top:1pt;padding-bottom:1pt;"><span id="S3.T2.5.17.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">DONE</span></td>
<td id="S3.T2.5.17.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_bb" style="padding-top:1pt;padding-bottom:1pt;">—</td>
<td id="S3.T2.5.17.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_bb" style="padding-top:1pt;padding-bottom:1pt;">Signal task successfully completed</td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>
</figure>
<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We formalize an autonomous agent interaction in MacArena as a Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xie et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bonatti et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, defined by the tuple <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{O},\mathcal{A},\mathcal{T},\Omega,r,\gamma,\mu_{0},\mathcal{G},p_{g},\varphi)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi><mo>,</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi><mo>,</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒜</mi><mo>,</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒯</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Ω</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>r</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>γ</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>μ</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒢</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>g</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>φ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{O},\mathcal{A},\mathcal{T},\Omega,r,\gamma,\mu_{0},\mathcal{G},p_{g},\varphi)</annotation></semantics></math>,
where <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{S}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{S}</annotation></semantics></math> is the full state space of the macOS environment (including hidden system states such as background processes and file system contents), <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{O}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{O}</annotation></semantics></math> is the observation space accessible to the agent (e.g., screenshots and accessibility trees), <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{A}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒜</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{A}</annotation></semantics></math> is the action space of mouse and keyboard interactions (full action space is listed in Table <a href="#S3.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 3.1 Problem Formulation ‣ 3 MacArena Environment ‣ MacArena: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on an Online macOS Environment" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>). <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{T}:\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}\rightarrow\mathcal{S}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒯</mi><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒜</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{T}:\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}\rightarrow\mathcal{S}</annotation></semantics></math> is the deterministic transition function, <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Omega" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">Ω</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Omega</annotation></semantics></math> is the observation function mapping states to observations, <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r:\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}\times\mathcal{G}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒜</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒢</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi>ℝ</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r:\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}\times\mathcal{G}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}</annotation></semantics></math> is the reward function, <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\gamma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>γ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\gamma</annotation></semantics></math> is the discount factor, <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mu_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>μ</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mu_{0}</annotation></semantics></math> is the initial state distribution, <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{G}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒢</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{G}</annotation></semantics></math> is the space of task goals (expressed as natural language instructions), <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{g}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>g</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{g}</annotation></semantics></math> is the distribution over goals, and <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\varphi:\mathcal{O}\rightarrow\mathcal{G}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>φ</mi><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒢</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\varphi:\mathcal{O}\rightarrow\mathcal{G}</annotation></semantics></math> is a mapping from observations to goals.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">At each timestep <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>, the agent receives an observation <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="o_{t}\in\mathcal{O}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>o</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">o_{t}\in\mathcal{O}</annotation></semantics></math> consisting of a screenshot of the current macOS desktop, optionally with the accessibility tree. Accessibility (a11y) is a structured, hierarchical representation of UI elements (buttons, text fields, menus) exposed by macOS via the Accessibility API, providing element labels, roles, and bounding boxes without requiring visual parsing. Based on this observation, the agent produces an executable action <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a_{t}\in\mathcal{A}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒜</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_{t}\in\mathcal{A}</annotation></semantics></math>, e.g., click. The action is executed within the virtual machine, transitioning the environment to a new state <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s_{t+1}\in\mathcal{S}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s_{t+1}\in\mathcal{S}</annotation></semantics></math> and yielding a new observation <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="o_{t+1}\in\mathcal{O}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>o</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">o_{t+1}\in\mathcal{O}</annotation></semantics></math>. This loop continues until the agent emits a terminal action (<span id="S3.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">DONE</span> or <span id="S3.SS1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">FAIL</span>) or the maximum number of steps is reached.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">MacArena implements an execution-based reward function <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r:\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}\times\mathcal{G}\rightarrow[0,1]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒜</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒢</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r:\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}\times\mathcal{G}\rightarrow[0,1]</annotation></semantics></math>. At the final step, a custom evaluation script compares the resulting environment state to the task objective and assigns a score, with higher values indicating greater task completion.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>Benchmark Structure</h3>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">MacArena consists of three core components: the environment, the tasks, and the evaluation framework.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Environment.</h4>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">MacArena runs inside virtual machines (VMs) managed by UTM<span id="footnote2" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup>
                <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">2</span>
                
                
                
                
                
                
                
              <a href="https://github.com/utmapp/UTM" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://github.com/utmapp/UTM</a></span></span></span>, which is built on Apple’s native Virtualization framework (see Appendix <a href="#A1" title="Appendix A Apple Virtualization Framework ‣ MacArena: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on an Online macOS Environment" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A</span></a> for details). We maintain two distinct VMs. The first is dedicated to tasks sourced from OSWorld and macOSWorld; it was configured manually to satisfy the setup assumptions of those benchmarks, including installed applications, system permissions, and verified evaluation conditions. The second VM is purpose-built for MacArena’s own tasks and is provisioned entirely via an automated build script. This approach eliminates manual configuration, simplifies migration across macOS versions, and makes it straightforward to add new applications in the future.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Since UTM does not natively support VM snapshot revert, we adopt a copy-on-use strategy: before each task episode, the original VM image is copied to a temporary instance used for the episode and discarded upon completion. This guarantees a clean, reproducible initial state for every evaluation run.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The environment exposes two types of observations to the agent: pixel-level screenshots and, optionally, the macOS accessibility tree taken using <span id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">macapptree</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Garkot et al., 2026</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Tasks.</h4>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">MacArena contains 421 tasks organized into two dimensions: application and task type, including cross-application workflows that require coordinating multiple macOS apps. Tasks are sourced from two existing benchmarks: OSWorld and macOSWorld, and supplemented with our own newly collected tasks, all reviewed by humans to ensure each task is executable, unambiguous, and correctly specified.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Each task is defined by three required components. The <span id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">instruction</span> field provides a natural language description of what the agent must accomplish. The <span id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">pre_command/config</span> field specifies an initialization procedure that prepares the VM for the task, such as downloading required files, launching applications, or opening documents. The <span id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">evaluator</span> field defines a deterministic function that programmatically verifies whether the task was completed successfully by inspecting the final environment state.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">MacArena supports two task formats inherited from its source benchmarks. The OSWorld format uses a set of predefined evaluation functions composed via a structured configuration file. The macOSWorld format uses shell scripts for both initialization and evaluation, offering greater flexibility for tasks that require more complex or platform-specific logic. Our own tasks follow both formats.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Evaluation Framework.</h4>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Task success in MacArena is determined by execution-based evaluation: after the agent emits a terminal action, the corresponding evaluator script is executed against the final VM state. Each evaluator returns a value in <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[0,1]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[0,1]</annotation></semantics></math> indicating how well the task was completed; the higher, the better. Evaluation criteria vary by task and may inspect file contents, application state, system properties, or the output of shell commands, depending on what the task requires.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Each of the 49 tasks in the MacArena subset is associated with a unique, hand-crafted evaluation script, yielding 49 distinct evaluation functions in total. This one-to-one correspondence between tasks and evaluators reflects the diversity of verification requirements
across macOS applications and task types.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.3 </span>Benchmark Statistics</h3>

<div id="S3.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">MacArena comprises 421 tasks in total, drawn from three sources: 221 tasks adapted from OSWorld, 151 tasks from macOSWorld, and 49 newly collected tasks across 5 categories for the MacArena-specific subset. The MacArena-specific subset spans 20 macOS applications. OSWorld and macOSWorld tasks retain their original application coverage, which includes both macOS-exclusive apps and cross-platform productivity tools.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Tasks are organized into 20 categories reflecting the structure of their source benchmarks. The OSWorld-derived tasks cover seven categories: <span id="S3.SS3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">chrome</span>, <span id="S3.SS3.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">gimp</span>, <span id="S3.SS3.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">libreoffice_calc</span>, <span id="S3.SS3.p2.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">libreoffice_writer</span>, <span id="S3.SS3.p2.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">thunderbird</span>, <span id="S3.SS3.p2.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">vs_code</span>, and <span id="S3.SS3.p2.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">multi_apps</span>. The macOSWorld-derived tasks span seven categories: <span id="S3.SS3.p2.1.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">sys_and_interface</span>, <span id="S3.SS3.p2.1.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">sys apps</span>, <span id="S3.SS3.p2.1.10" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">file management</span>, <span id="S3.SS3.p2.1.11" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">productivity</span>, <span id="S3.SS3.p2.1.12" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">media</span>, <span id="S3.SS3.p2.1.13" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">multi apps</span>, and <span id="S3.SS3.p2.1.14" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">advanced</span>. The MacArena-specific tasks are organized into 5 categories, inheriting macOSWorld names: <span id="S3.SS3.p2.1.15" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">file management</span>, <span id="S3.SS3.p2.1.16" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">system and interface</span>, <span id="S3.SS3.p2.1.17" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">advanced apps</span>, <span id="S3.SS3.p2.1.18" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">built-in apps</span>, and <span id="S3.SS3.p2.1.19" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">productivity</span>, covering tasks that require interaction with a single macOS application at a time.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S3.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 3.3 Benchmark Statistics ‣ 3 MacArena Environment ‣ MacArena: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on an Online macOS Environment" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> shows the distribution of tasks across all 20 categories, illustrating the diversity of macOS use cases covered by MacArena.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F2" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2606.06560v1/distribution.png" id="S3.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/373;" width="476" height="373" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S3.F2.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 2</span>: </span><span id="S3.F2.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Distribution of tasks per category across the full MacArena benchmark.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Experiments</h2>

<figure id="S4.T3" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S4.T3.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 3</span>: </span><span id="S4.T3.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Success rates (%) of baseline agents on MacArena.
Best result in each row is <span id="S4.T3.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">bold</span>.</span></figcaption>
<table id="S4.T3.6" class="ltx_tabular ltx_centering ltx_guessed_headers ltx_align_middle">
<tbody class="ltx_tbody">
<tr id="S4.T3.6.1" class="ltx_tr">

<td id="S4.T3.6.28.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb ltx_border_t" style="padding-left:5.0pt;padding-right:5.0pt;">21.14</td>

<td id="S4.T3.6.28.5" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb ltx_border_t" style="padding-left:5.0pt;padding-right:5.0pt;"><span id="S4.T3.6.28.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">31.83</span></td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>
</figure>
<div id="S4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate four baseline agents on MacArena: UI-TARS-1.5 7B <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qin et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, Qwen3-VL 2B, Qwen3-VL 4B <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Team, 2025</a>)</cite>, and OpenAI Computer Use Preview <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">OpenAI, 2025</a>)</cite>. All agents interact with the macOS virtual machine through raw mouse and keyboard actions. Each agent receives a screenshot of the current desktop at every step. Each task is limited to 15 steps, and each model has 2 runs. Task success is determined by execution-based evaluation scripts as described in Section <a href="#S3.SS2" title="3.2 Benchmark Structure ‣ 3 MacArena Environment ‣ MacArena: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on an Online macOS Environment" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.2</span></a>. We report Success Rate (SR) as the primary metric, defined as the percentage of tasks for which the evaluation script returns a positive result.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#S4.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ MacArena: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on an Online macOS Environment" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> reports the success rates of all four agents across the three subsets and 16 task categories. OpenAI Computer Use Preview achieves the highest overall success rate of 31.83%, followed by Qwen3-VL 4B (24.23%), UI-TARS-1.5 7B (21.14%), and Qwen3-VL 2B (11.40%).</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>macOS vs. Linux Performance Gap</h3>

<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">A key motivation for MacArena is the hypothesis that macOS presents distinct challenges for GUI agents beyond what existing Linux-based benchmarks capture. To investigate this, we compare model performance on the OSWorld subset of MacArena against officially reported scores on the original OSWorld benchmark, which runs on Ubuntu Linux with a 15-step budget. Table <a href="#S4.T4" title="Table 4 ‣ 4.1 macOS vs. Linux Performance Gap ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ MacArena: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on an Online macOS Environment" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> presents this comparison for models where official scores are publicly available.</p>
</div>

</table>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Both models with available reference scores show a meaningful drop when evaluated on macOS, despite the task set being identical. This gap is due to macOS introducing platform-specific differences in application appearance, keyboard shortcuts, window management, and system behavior that models trained primarily on Linux and Windows trajectories are not adapted to. The consistent degradation across both models suggests that macOS poses a genuinely harder environment for current GUI agents.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2 </span>Analysis</h3>

<section id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Multi-app tasks.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The multi-app tasks category involves interaction between 2 or more applications. This category remains the hardest category across all models and both the OSWorld and macOSWorld subsets, with most agents scoring at or near 0%. This is consistent with prior work <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xie et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2025</a>)</cite> and indicates that coordinating across applications remains an open challenge even for state-of-the-art models.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Category-level strengths and weaknesses.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">UI-TARS-1.5 7B achieves the highest scores on VS Code (68.42%) and OS tasks (50.00%) within the OSWorld subset, suggesting stronger adaptation to terminal and code editing workflows. In contrast, it performs poorly on macOS-native categories such as Advanced (0.00%) and MacArena (10.2%), indicating limited exposure to macOS-specific application patterns during training. OpenAI CUA dominates the macOSWorld subset, particularly System Apps (71.88%) and Productivity (70.00%), reflecting stronger adaptation to native macOS applications.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Divergence between OSWorld and MacArena subsets.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">An interesting reversal emerges when comparing performance on the OSWorld subset against the MacArena-specific subset. UI-TARS-1.5 7B outperforms OpenAI CUA on the OSWorld subset (21.27% vs. 16.74%), yet this advantage completely inverts on the MacArena-specific tasks, where OpenAI CUA scores 36.73% against UI-TARS-1.5 7B’s 10.2%, a gap of over 26.5 percentage points in the opposite direction. This divergence suggests that strong performance on tasks originally designed for Linux does not transfer to novel macOS-native tasks. UI-TARS-1.5 7B likely benefits from having seen OSWorld-style tasks or similar Linux-based GUI trajectories during training, which gives it an advantage on the OSWorld subset despite the platform shift. However, when faced with genuinely new macOS applications and interaction patterns in the MacArena subset, this advantage disappears entirely. OpenAI CUA, by contrast, appears to have broader macOS-specific knowledge, possibly from training on diverse real-world computer use data that includes macOS. This result highlights an important limitation of evaluating GUI agents exclusively on existing benchmarks: a model can appear competitive by pattern-matching previously seen task structures while failing to generalize to new environments. MacArena’s own task subset is specifically designed to surface this gap.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Task difficulty via step consumption.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To further characterize the relative difficulty of each subset, we analyze the average number of steps consumed per task by OpenAI CUA, the best-performing model in our evaluation. We report both the average steps across all tasks and the average steps on completed tasks only, as the latter reflects the true complexity of tasks the model was capable of solving. Table <a href="#S4.T5" title="Table 5 ‣ Task difficulty via step consumption. ‣ 4.2 Analysis ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ MacArena: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on an Online macOS Environment" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> summarizes these statistics aggregated by subset.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.T5" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S4.T5.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 5</span>: </span><span id="S4.T5.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Average steps consumed by OpenAI CUA per subset, across all tasks, and only on completed tasks.</span></figcaption>

<th id="S4.T5.5.1.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_border_tt"><span id="S4.T5.5.1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Avg. Steps (All)</span></th>

</table>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The macOSWorld subset has the lowest average step consumption across all tasks (10.92) and on completed tasks (8.05), indicating that its tasks are, on average, shorter and less complex than those in the other two subsets. This provides a quantitative explanation for why models achieve higher success rates on macOSWorld: beyond any potential platform familiarity, the tasks themselves require fewer interaction steps to complete. The OSWorld subset requires more steps on average (13.88 overall, 11.08 for completed tasks). The MacArena-specific subset exhibits the highest step consumption of all three, both overall (13.96) and on completed tasks (12.69).</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Limitations and Future Work</h2>

<section id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Automatic task generation.</h4>

<div id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">All tasks in MacArena were manually created by human annotators, which is
time-consuming and limits scalability. A promising direction for future work
is to automate task generation by leveraging LLMs to synthesize diverse,
plausible task instructions, potentially guided by
application-specific schemas or interaction logs. However, automatically
generated tasks introduce quality concerns: instructions may be ambiguous,
infeasible, or trivially easy. Ensuring that generated tasks are valid,
non-redundant, and appropriately challenging would therefore require either
human validation or automated feasibility checks, for example, by verifying
that a reference agent can complete the task within a bounded number of
steps. Addressing this pipeline would substantially reduce annotation cost
and enable MacArena to scale to a broader range of applications and task
types.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Human performance baseline.</h4>

<div id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">While tasks in MacArena are 100% human-verified and each task is possible to do, benchmark does not currently include a human performance study. Establishing human baselines would provide an important reference point for interpreting model results and understanding the remaining headroom for future improvement, as done in OSWorld <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xie et al., 2024</a>)</cite> and macOSWorld <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Use of LLMs.</h4>

<div id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Parts of this work were refined using LLMs for better readability and structure.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S6" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">6 </span>Conclusion</h2>

<div id="S6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We presented MacArena, a benchmark for evaluating GUI agents on macOS, comprising 421 tasks drawn from OSWorld and macOSWorld, as well as a newly collected set of 49 macOS-native tasks spanning 20 applications. MacArena provides a unified evaluation framework that runs all tasks within a reproducible virtual machine environment using execution-based evaluation scripts, enabling direct comparison of agent behavior across task origins on a single platform.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Our evaluation of agents reveals that macOS remains a challenging and underexplored environment for current GUI agents. All models with available reference scores perform worse on the same task set when evaluated on macOS compared to the original Linux-based OSWorld environment, confirming that the platform gap is real. Furthermore, relative model rankings shift substantially depending on which subset of MacArena is examined: a model that leads on OSWorld-derived tasks can fall far behind on novel macOS-native tasks. This suggests that strong performance on existing benchmarks may reflect familiarity with specific task distributions rather than genuine cross-platform GUI understanding, and that macOS-native tasks are necessary to expose this limitation.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p3.1" class="ltx_p">MacArena is designed to serve as a foundation for GUI agents that generalize reliably across operating systems, and to establish macOS as a first-class evaluation target alongside Linux and Windows.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="Sx1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section">Impact Statement</h2>

<div id="Sx1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This paper introduces a benchmark for evaluating computer-use agents on macOS. The primary goal is to advance the scientific study of GUI agents by providing a more comprehensive and reproducible evaluation environment. We do not anticipate direct negative societal consequences specific to this work. Improvements in agent capabilities enabled by better evaluation tools may contribute to automating knowledge work, with socioeconomic implications widely discussed in the AI community. We do not believe these consequences require specific highlighting here beyond what is already widely discussed in the context of autonomous agent research.</p>
</div>
</section>

<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
<section id="A1" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix A </span>Apple Virtualization Framework</h2>

<div id="A1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">MacArena is built on Apple’s Virtualization framework<span id="footnote3" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">3</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">3</sup>
            <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">3</span>
            
            
            
            
            
            
            
          <a href="https://developer.apple.com/documentation/virtualization" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://developer.apple.com/documentation/virtualization</a></span></span></span>, a native hypervisor API introduced in macOS 11 (Big Sur) that enables the creation and management of virtual machines directly on Apple Silicon hardware. Unlike traditional virtualization solutions such as QEMU, which rely on software emulation, the framework leverages the hardware virtualization extensions of M-series chips to run guest operating systems at near-native performance.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">A key practical constraint of the framework is that Apple Silicon hosts can run at most two macOS guest VMs simultaneously — a hard limit enforced at the system level. This restricts the degree of parallelism available per machine and is an important consideration for benchmark throughput. In MacArena, we account for this by running up to two evaluation tasks in parallel on a single host. To scale evaluation further, multiple host machines can be employed independently, as the per-host VM limit does not preclude distributed execution across several Apple Silicon machines.</p>
</div>
</section>
</article>
